customize.text: Character Stories

<color=#ffd680>Ashru</color>
Back when Nefer negotiated with the Ibis King, stranded as the latter was in Aaru, the king sent her his emissary: a small cat named Ashru.
Through the body of this little creature, the king was able to have a brief meeting with her despite his circumstances.
Interestingly, while indwelling Ashru's body, the Ibis King seemed to also share in the cat's physical sensations.
Unfortunately, before Nefer could learn about this, the cunning king had already left Ashru's body, turning him back into an ordinary little cat.
As for the reason Nefer has kept Ashru by her side...
Besides the fact that he is truly adorable...
The owner of the Curatorium of Secrets has considered that the Ibis King might once again use Ashru's body to communicate with her...
And when that time comes, she will never let such a golden opportunity slip away again...
<color=#ffd680>Moon Wheel</color>
"...That is quite the bargaining chip, Lady Nefer."
The emissary from the Northern Intelligence Network nodded. Nefer's proposal, in truth, had exceeded his expectations. He had merely hoped the Curatorium's owner would help locate a certain traitor so that the appropriate punishment could be meted out. But at the meeting, he learned that she had already arranged for their target to visit the Curatorium for some business three days later, giving them the perfect opportunity to act. It was as if she had known his intentions all along.
And as for Nefer's requested recompense, it was simply "to have a chat with the person in charge."
The visitor thought of the aging representative, an influential figure at the Northern Intelligence Network who had long been searching for a successor. This visit to the Curatorium, this very deal, had been approved by him. Could it be that he had already—
Perhaps this conversation between Nefer and the representative would lead to a change in leadership at the Network...
The emissary quietly pushed down certain thoughts that might stir up unnecessary trouble, offered his thanks to Nefer, and took his leave.
...
Nefer caught the Moon Wheel that she had tossed high into the air as she watched the emissary depart.
It had appeared at the bottom of the box of gifts the emissary brought after their conversation. Amidst the pearls and the gold, this extraordinary item immediately caught her eye — it was something no mortal could have forged, and it certainly wasn't listed in the emissary's official inventory.
But what really made her pause to think was another story about the moon from the past.
Long ago, she had held a conversation with the Lord of Lies within Aaru, and to this day, she still recalled how skilled that sycophant, the Ibis King, was at deception and persuasion. She still remembered how he boasted of laboring across three moons such that he might guide the benighted mortals below, weaving reasonable threads of fate for all living things, such that life on earth could sprout anew in cycles. He had also told her how, upon arriving in Sumeru, his talents were recognized by the discerning King Deshret. He claimed that he was then elevated to lead the great "Seven Pillars of King Deshret," that he drank the wine of revelry with the king himself, and that he once planted greenery alongside the Goddess of Flowers. In short, if Nefer were to accept his grace, she would gain extraordinary power.
Nefer didn't believe these tales for a moment, absurd as they were. To her, they were nothing more than lies hastily spun by an old trickster trying to win her trust. After all, King Deshret had exiled three sycophantic courtiers to Aaru. Would it not have been all too easy for the trio, extraordinary as they nonetheless were, to come together in the time since and weave a story meant to deceive the unsuspecting?
"Will you truly refuse to believe anything?" Thoth, inhabiting the cat’s body, asked angrily. The cat's fur bristled, not from conscious effort, but simply because cat fur naturally stands on end when they're upset.
"If a deity wishes to deceive people with their wisdom, the people will surely be deceived," Nefer responded with a shrug. "So I won't believe a single word you say either."
"But the power you're about to give me? That's worth believing in," said the dispossessed desert dweller with a smile. "Today, I own nothing, and as such, there's nothing else I can believe in."
...
Nefer fiddled with the Moon Wheel with the slightest hint of a smile on her face.
...It seemed there was a tiny bit of truth hidden somewhere in all of Thoth's lies.
A moment later, she tossed this long-overdue gift into a document bag.
This extraordinary item should serve as a powerful deterrent at the meeting three days down the line.
Voice-Over

<color=#ffd680>About Us: Inner Thoughts</color>
Most people are incapable of hiding their true feelings. As long as I watch their faces closely, I can see right through them. And when I can't? That's when Thoth's little blessing comes in handy... Hah, just kidding. To this day, I've never met anyone I couldn't read like a book.
<color=#ffd680>About the Moon Wheel</color>
Maybe there really is some mysterious link between Thoth and the moon, and that's why I ended up with this thing. But I wouldn't exactly say it feels like "the gaze of the gods" — more like the gaze of that old trickster, watching my every step from behind. Not that I have any proof, of course, but... Heh, I guess a good liar is always afraid of being lied to themselves.
<color=#ffd680>Nefer's Troubles</color>
I still haven't found the answer Thoth needs, and I must say — being led around by someone else, mortal or divine, is not a particularly pleasant experience. The Ibis King seemed to find my response amusing enough, it's just a shame that it wasn't the "correct" answer King Deshret was looking for. Then again, if I ever do find it, Thoth will be set free... and frankly, I'm not too keen on the idea of handing over such a precious gift on a silver platter, least of all to that old swindler. So there it is... a classic lose-lose situation.

<color=#ffd680>About Moon Envoys</color>
<color=#99ffff>Zibai</color> : I was once an angel — a member of a race tasked with guiding humanity. Then, graced by serendipity, I became a moon envoy.

<color=#99ffff>Zibai</color> : Of course not. Though my memories are still hazy, I vaguely remember some of my colleagues — there was one who liked to take on the form of an ibis...

Ibis King

Several millennia ago, when there was no Archon in Sumeru, the desert was ruled by
a king of warriors, horticulturists, and sages. He controlled the winds whistling through the desert, the dunes turned bright silver by moonlight, and the one thousand and one Jinn who hid within the night and the calls of owls. He led his people to prosperity and to pursue the limits of wisdom, relying on seven wise retainers, the Seven Pillars. Among them was the right hand of King Deshret, the head of the Seven Sages, the minister of ministers — the Goat King, Heryshaf; the great bird winging skyward towards the sun, the King's soul — the saint Bennu; the lioness with a human head, the King's will — the saint Shesepankh; the dragon who obtained the flesh and blood of the King, who never counted itself among the Seven — Apep; the Captain of Captains — the Crocodile King, Sobek; the wisest of sages — Hermanubis; and the Scribe of Scribes — the moon envoy, Ibis King, Thoth. Thoth represented the wisest aspects of King Deshret, inventing the desert script and arcane arts at his king's command. According to legend, the Ibis King was the keeper of records and the secret envoy of the moon and stars, but among people, he had a reputation as a deceiver. Al-Ahmar watched them speak of the present and the future, of the wisdom they possessed or were about to obtain. The Seven Pillars were his proud retainers, confident in their belief that, so long as each one of them used their abilities to the fullest, progress was inevitable. Yet, King Deshret's ambition was not destined to be allowed in a closed-off world such as this, so nothing went as planned.

After King Deshret's companion, the
sacrificed herself to open the way to forbidden knowledge for Al-Ahmar, three of his closest retainers approached the king with proposals. The flattering Goat King said it was improper to indulge in dreams of old and sorrows of the past. The endless power and wisdom of their land could build King Deshret a palace that surpasses the heavens and bring people a prosperous future. But Al-Ahmar frowned and refused, and the Goat King fell silent. The Ibis King advised that divine punishment of a thousand years past brought the downfall of wisdom and history. Only those who control the past can create a bright future. In the present oasis, the wisdom of the "present" was hidden. But if they wanted to seize the "past," they had to act swiftly. Al-Ahmar struck the ground with his staff and refused, and the Ibis King fell silent. The King of Crocodiles was the last to address King Deshret. He said that if they were to recall the lost lives, to welcome lost opportunities and dreams back into the fold, this was their final chance. The greater the authority, the greater the emptiness. The greater the wisdom, the greater the sorrow. Compared to the emptiness of delusion, only resurrection and immortal life could mend the endless pit of regret. Al-Ahmar fell silent and then replied, <color=#ffffffd9>"Fine."</color>

King Deshret heeded the deceptive words of his three retainers. He built a huge maze for his kingdom, before trapping himself deep within it in search of forbidden knowledge and an elixir with which he might abandon his mortal form. But this led not to the desert's prosperity, but to its collapse. Desert legend holds that in just one night, the kingdom of wisdom and power was buried by the sands of retribution. They say Al-Ahmar separated his mind from his flesh and bone, placing it within the corridors, stairways, doorways, and beams that crawled eternally into the depths. It is said that Al-Ahmar's body gradually decayed on his throne while worms feasted on it, and that his soul merged into one with the wailing souls of the millions in his kingdom, doomed to wander, lost amidst the howling end, traveling along the dark and winding corridors, growing ever closer to the bottomless abyss. Thus did the great civilization Al-Ahmar built fall by his own hand.

customize.text: Riddles

Even before the Flower Goddess disappeared, she left King Deshret three riddles to which he didn't know the answer. After her death, when life grew unbearable for the king, he locked his three deceitful retainers, the Ibis King, the Goat King, and the Crocodile King, in Aaru — the far side of eternity, the final land of dreams for all desert dwellers. He told the Ibis King that he could be freed from his eternal curse if he chose people who could give the correct answers to these three questions.
The first to catch Thoth's eye was Goudarz, a young noble who dreamed of freeing his countrymen from the shackles of slavery. He stepped into the sacred hall buried deep beneath the sands to meet the Ibis King. Thoth promised that if Goudarz answered one of the riddles, he would grant him power over men.
And so, the wisest of them all among the sage monks spoke thusly:

<color=#ffffffd9>"What rises and falls in endless turns, perishing at its apex before swelling once more?"</color>
<color=#ffffffd9>"Like the moon, it waxes full, then wanes away into nothing."</color>
<color=#ffffffd9>"Both the wise and the foolish yearn for it, in ceaseless cycles of desire."</color>
<color=#ffffffd9>"Yet like the tides, it ebbs and flows within the hearts of men."</color>
The young Goudarz answered thusly:

<color=#ffffffd9>"What you speak of is conspiracy and treachery. The robes of those who speak idly of virtue conceal nothing but festering weakness and fatigue."</color>
<color=#ffffffd9>"It is this very weakness that brought down the sapphire domes, and it is this very weakness that has driven the people to cry out in sorrow."</color>

The Ibis King found his answer quite interesting, so he bestowed upon him the power to "deceive" and handed him the Staff of Falsehoods. The name "Goudarz" gradually became lost to history, replaced by the mighty title of King Saleb Dowleh. The warrior who once would tolerate no lies had gained kingly power through cunning, casting the illusion of a golden age over the fading hues of twilight. At the end of his life, he again heard the voice of the Ibis King, who asked him again: <color=#ffffffd9>"What causes our rise and fall?"</color> The aged ruler replied that he could only speak lies, which he himself no longer trusted. He no longer wished to lead his people, so he told Thoth to seek the answer in his own blood. Then power was seized by other tribes, until ultimately all the kingdoms crumbled to dust, scattered across the world by the desert winds. And, as if collecting moonlight like amber honey, the Ibis King had taken the king's last will as his final answer.

The Ibis King posed his second riddle to Makhaira, the Jinn-blooded dancing girl who had once been given as a gift to the tyrant king of Gurabad. The Ibis King asked her, <color=#ffffffd9>"What obliterates love and hate?"</color> She replied, <color=#ffffffd9>"I have nothing left to lose. Vengeance alone can quench both love and hate."</color> He found this answer fascinating, so he granted her the power to "be loved." According to legend, through her ruthless sword dance, she won the king's favor, as well as the prince's attention. When the tyrant fell asleep after yet another feast, the "Temptress of Woe" polished her sword and prepared for one final dance. The young prince approached Makhaira, asking her to do something for the greatness of the old country that had long since fallen. The lovers hatched a plot to overthrow the ruler, so that the prince would gain the throne and Makhaira would no longer have to flatter others. The tyrant thus returned to the land of searing sands in an ugly fashion, and the great cause of conquering kingdoms and harems finally vanished into thin air. After getting her vengeance, the concubine reigned as queen for many years, until her enemies attempted a coup, and she chose snake venom to take her own life.

The Ibis King wanted to ask his third riddle to a young man named
who had come to his temple with a scholar from the Sumeru Akademiya. Zandik was exceedingly clever but was also mistrustful and narcissistic in equal measure, and there did not seem to be a line he was unwilling to cross. Thus, Thoth hesitated to give him the third gift. Too much power could be dangerous in the hands of someone like him, so the Ibis King found himself rather relieved when Zandik declined the gift, as he didn't need it. Zandik himself believed that people like Thoth, who only talk about benefits and never mention the cost, are a dime a dozen at the Grand Bazaar. As he refused, the Ibis King saw contempt and disdain radiating from his gaze and sensed that close association with such a man would lead to nothing good. The companion from the Akademiya was exhausted, and Thoth feared that Zandik might leave him behind or that some other "accident" might befall him. So, the Ibis King concocted a lie: he claimed that only the descendants of Tulaytullah, of whom the scholar was one, were allowed to come and go from the temple. Without him, Zandik would have no escape.

Although Thoth did not utter the riddle to Zandik, the temple was discovered several centuries later by the desert dweller, Nefer. As a child, her entire tribe, including her father, the chief, was wiped out by another tribe due to a dispute over a well of water. With the help of other desert dwellers, she was able to enter the Sumeru Akademiya, but because of her origins, she was treated with disdain. Realizing that her father had tried to ask the Akademiya for help, but they did not care, Nefer left the Akademiya and took revenge on the tribe that had killed her family. When she returned to her home village, it was in ruins, and only the temple of the Ibis King stood untouched, as if neither war nor sandstorms could shake it. Near the temple, the woman noticed a black kitten, which served as a vessel for the spirit of Thoth. The cat, Ashru, led her to the heart of the temple, where the Ibis King struck a deal with her and posed a riddle: <color=#ffffffd9>"What determines truth and falsehood?"</color>

Nefer's answer seemed convincing enough to Thoth, so he rewarded her with a special chess set that was capable of revealing secrets. But her answer was not what Al-Ahmar wanted, so Thoth remained imprisoned in Aaru, and now he can only wait for the woman to give the correct answer. And although Nefer does not know whether Goudarz and Makhaira's answers sealed their fate, or whether their end was determined by the power bestowed upon them, she is in no hurry to seek the correct answer. She took the cat, Ashru, possessed by Thoth, with her, believing that the Ibis King would one day contact her again. Furthermore, thanks to the Ibis King's connection with the moon, Nefer received the Lunar Wheel. But instead of the gods' gaze, she feels as if she is being watched by an old deceiver.

customize.text: How many moons are there in the sky?

One day, a member of the Temple of Silence, Djer, went exploring in the desert and fell into quicksand, falling into the ruins of the temple. In a panic, he tripped over a device, and in a brief moment, his mind was overwhelmed by a flood of information his brain couldn't process. Suddenly, he heard a male voice saying, <color=#ffffffd9>"Don't eat Ajilenakh Nuts,"</color> and the phrase began repeating endlessly in Djer's head. He also heard a cat's meow, which led him outside. A similar story happened to the student from the Rtawahist Darshan of Sumeru Akademiya, Layla, who went stargazing and fell through the sand into the same ruins. Her mind was also flooded with knowledge until a male voice suddenly asked her, <color=#ffffffd9>"How many moons are there in the sky?"</color> Then, like Djer, a cat's meow showed her the way out.

To discover the truth about what was happening, the head of the Temple of Silence, Sethos, and Layla's friends set out for the temple. Inside, they discovered the device that Djer and Layla had touched, but it was already out of energy. Deeper in the temple, they discovered tablets left by ancient priests that told the story of Goudarz and Makhaira. Then they saw a cat, the vessel of the Ibis King. This temple had once been dedicated to Thoth, but later came to belong to the descendants of the cats he had once raised. The Ibis King, imprisoned in Aaru, was unable to freely communicate with humans, so he assumed the form of a cat to communicate with the humans who occasionally entered the temple.

It turned out that the Ibis King himself had helped Layla and Djer escape the ruins. They had accidentally activated a device that King Deshret had once used to measure human brain power. This contact flooded their minds with more knowledge than they could handle, so Thoth replaced it with simpler, more repetitive information. But the side effect was that the same thought began to repeat itself in their heads over and over again. Neither the phrase about nuts nor the phrase about the number of moons held any deep meaning for the Ibis King, even though he knew there had once been three moons in the sky. As he bid farewell to Sethos, Layla, and their friends, the Ibis King asked for King Deshret's device to be deactivated and went off to play chess with the Crocodile King in Aaru.

customize.text: Legends

There are a few legends about the deceiving King Deshret's retainers in Sumeru. One of them tells people not to trust the meek, nor the wise, nor those who shed tears. According to this legend, the tame and kind sheep chief sent seven lambs to look for the freshest grassy meadows and water. The wise bird ran into the seven lambs and asked them where they were headed, and the lambs told the bird their goal. They asked the bird, which could see everything from the height, to lead them to the meadow, but the bird wanted to wash and groom its feathers in a meadow with a water source, so it led them in the wrong direction. The lambs headed north and met a crocodile covered in armor. The crocodile shed tears in sympathy for the lambs' plight and decided to escort them back to their homeland. On their way back, the wise bird ran into the lambs again and was astonished by the crocodile's kindness, so it decided to accompany them. When they reached the lambs' home, the crocodile opened its huge maw and ate them all. The crocodile shed tears once again and spoke of the tameness and kindness of the sheep chief.

Although the real Ibis King prefers chess to cards, another legend about the Ibis King and the Crocodile King was written for the card game, Genius Invokation TCG. In one chapter of the book, the Crocodile King and the Ibis King were arguing ceaselessly, and one day their argument turned to the changing of things. Sobek sought a person who, having received the blessing of an Oceanid, could turn any liquid into wine. Thoth brought a person who, under the influence of a curse, turned everything into silver. The King Deshret's sages bet on which effect would win out in the end and asked the leader of the priestly class. Hermanubis, to make a conjecture as to the eventual result. <color=#ffffffd9>"Both forms of power clash directly, as sharp spears striking sturdy shields,"</color> said Hermanubis, <color=#ffffffd9>"And they must each yield unto the other, and take a step back. This is the principle of equilibrium."</color> In the end, the final result was that the cup became pure silver, while the silted water within became a fine liquor with suspended grains of silver. Yet the Crocodile King and Ibis King did not understand Hermanubis's admonishment, instead continuing their battle. In the end, they invented a strange summoning magic. And now, the two of them have traversed millennia to continue their battle upon the field of Genius Invokation TCG.

When the final volume of King of Invokations #1 was released, a special pre-order was supposed to include a sample product in the form of a weapon called the Ibis Piercer. Due to its unique specifications, the request to produce a sample was misunderstood as one to craft an actual weapon, which upset the Yae Publishing House. However, Fukumoto, who was present when the bow was delivered, was impressed by this turn of events and wrote a story that was later included in the book as an appendix. According to the story, the bow, decorated with precious stones, was once in the treasury of the Ibis King. The Crocodile King was confident that whoever wielded this bow would become the most skilled archer under King Deshret, so he was determined to obtain the bow at all costs. The prussian green-skinned young man asked if he could obtain the bow if he became the most brilliant archer of all, but was only met with a smirk in response. When King Deshret had long disappeared, the Crocodile King decided to trample the sea of sands in the name of the "Rite of Duels," all to erase the barriers between the multitude of worlds and thus incite a frenzied war. To stop him, a
holding a golden bow climbed the steps leading to the ritual. After this battle, Sobek was sealed by Thoth in the "Room of Duels" for his thirst for a great war and his attempt to destroy the walls of the worlds. The "Room of Duels" was like some kind of sanctuary: it was impossible to escape from with no cheat going unnoticed. Even the Crocodile King could not leave this place.

Several centuries later, a young man named Abu discovered the Casket of Tomes. The Crocodile King possessed him, and together, they became the king of invokation. When Sobek entered the sealed "Room of Duels" again, using the young man, he saw a longbow held by the phantom. It was as if time stood still, so that the remnant of his soul could pass through the shattered doors and scattered corridors, and return to the chamber of treachery and machinations. Grasping the inescapable golden arrow fired off by the Bow of Secret Rites that was zipping towards him, he saved the body from an unfortunate fate of being impaled through the chest. But at this moment, the secret ritual dissipated, the arrow was dispelled, and the silhouette of the bow-wielder vanished in a flash. Sobek grabbed the longbow before it clattered to the ground. His multiple attempts at seizing this gold-forged bow had ended in failure, which contributed to the rift between him and the Ibis King. Alas, when he finally acquired the treasure that he had long coveted, he found that his heart was as cold as a stagnant swamp, with nary a ripple of joy. The Crocodile King pondered and concluded that he no longer had such a great yearning to satisfy those unfulfilled desires as he did in his youth.
